function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on what you’re trying to analyse, the sample matrix, the required sensitivity, and the downstream instrumentation. Below is a quick guide to help you decide which technique might suit your needs best.** | Ionisation Technique | Typical Use‑Cases | Strengths | Weaknesses | When to Pick It | |----------------------|-------------------|-----------|------------|-----------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Small, volatile, thermally stable molecules (e.g., hydrocarbons, pesticides). | • Robust, reproducible fragmentation patterns.
• Good for library matching.
• No matrix effects. | • Requires gas‑phase molecules; not suitable for large biomolecules.
• Hard ionisation can lead to extensive fragmentation. | • GC‑MS workflows where you need a universal, well‑characterised ionisation source. | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Semi‑volatile organics, compounds that fragment too much under EI. | • Softer than EI → less fragmentation.
• Can produce protonated or deprotonated ions.
• Useful for quantitative work. | • Requires a reagent gas (CH₄, NH₃, etc.).
• Less universal fragmentation libraries. | • When you need a softer ionisation but still use GC‑MS. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Small to medium polar molecules, pharmaceuticals, environmental contaminants. | • Works with a wide range of polarities.
• Compatible with LC‑MS.
• Good for high‑throughput screening. | • Less effective for very large biomolecules.
• Requires a nebuliser and corona discharge. | • LC‑MS of small molecules where you need a robust, “one‑size‑fits‑all” source. | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Large biomolecules (proteins, peptides, nucleic acids), metabolites, complex mixtures. | • Very soft ionisation → preserves non‑covalent complexes.
• Produces multiply charged ions → extends mass range.
• Excellent for LC‑MS/MS. | • Susceptible to ion suppression from salts or detergents.
• Requires careful optimisation of solvent composition. | • Proteomics, metabolomics, or any workflow that needs to detect large, labile molecules. | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteins, peptides, polymers, large biomolecules, imaging mass spectrometry. | • Minimal sample prep.
• High throughput.
• Good for imaging (MALDI‑IMS). | • Limited to molecules that can be co‑crystallised with a matrix.
• Lower resolution compared to ESI‑MS/MS. | • Protein sequencing, peptide mapping, imaging of tissue sections. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | Non‑polar, aromatic compounds, PAHs, some pharmaceuticals. | • Works well for non‑polar analytes that are hard to ionise with APCI/ESI.
• Can be coupled to LC‑MS. | • Requires a UV lamp and sometimes a dopant.
• Less common, fewer commercial sources. | • When you need to ionise non‑polar compounds that give poor signals in APCI/ESI. | | **Laser Ablation Electrospray Ionisation (LAESI)** | Direct sampling of solid or liquid samples (e.g., tissues, food). | • Minimal sample prep.
• Ambient ionisation.
• Good for imaging. | • Requires laser ablation hardware.
• Lower sensitivity than MALDI/ESI. | • Rapid screening of solid samples without extraction. | ### Quick Decision Flow 1. **What is the size of your analyte?** - *Small (<500 Da)* → EI or CI (GC‑MS) or APCI/APPI (LC‑MS). - *Large (>500 Da)* → ESI or MALDI (LC‑MS or MALDI‑TOF). 2. **Do you need to preserve non‑covalent complexes?** - Yes → ESI. - No → Any of the above. 3. **Is the sample highly polar or non‑polar?** - Polar → ESI/APCI. - Non‑polar → APPI or EI/CI. 4. **Do you need imaging or spatial localisation?** - Yes → MALDI‑IMS or LAESI. - No → Standard LC‑MS/MS or GC‑MS. 5. **What is your throughput requirement?** - High throughput → MALDI or ESI (fast LC‑MS). - Low throughput, detailed structural info → EI/CI (library matching) or ESI‑MS/MS. ### Bottom Line - **For routine small‑molecule screening**: *GC‑MS with EI* (or CI if you need softer ionisation). - **For complex, polar, or large biomolecules**: *LC‑MS with ESI* (or APCI for smaller polar molecules). - **For imaging or rapid solid‑sample analysis**: *MALDI‑IMS* or *LAESI*. - **For non‑polar, aromatic compounds**: *APPI* (if available). If you can share more specifics about your sample type, matrix, and analytical goals, I can narrow down the recommendation even further!
